newsitem.title: INDIA: INDIAN COPPER FIRM TURNAROUND LINKED TO COSTS.
newsitem.headline: INDIAN COPPER FIRM TURNAROUND LINKED TO COSTS.

text.p: India's state-owned monolith, Hindustan Copper Ltd (HCL) will have to cut staff and trim mining costs if it is to win a strategic partner to aid a turnaround, analysts said on Thursday.
India's Disinvestment Commission said in a report on Wednesday that HCL could seek a strategic partner as part of a phased strategy for partial privatisation.

In order for HCL to survive, plans to increase smelter and refining capacity at Khetri in the northern state of Rajasthan to 100,000 tonnes from the existing 31,000 tonnes, must be implemented immediately, the commission said.
"In terms of a foreign or Indian partner, it will depend on how viable will it be for the partner," a Bombay-based analyst who wished to remain anonymous said.
Analysts said potential partners would scrutinise several factors including the rate of ore recovery and mining costs.
HCL's current production and conversion costs were unviable and it had inherent problems like over-staffing, they said.

"HCL has to depend on its own copper mines which have a poor metal content, but it has to put up with LME(London Metal Exchange) price fluctuation," said an analyst at a brokerage, who did not want to be named.
But M. Vishwanathan of the Calcutta-based Indian Copper Development Centre said HCL had captive mines and a well-laid out infrastructure that could help any potential partner.
"HCL can do addition in capacity at a fraction of a cost compared to other greenfield smelters," said Vishwanathan. "If they can manage well, the future is not bad for HCL at all."
He said HCL needed to increase the capacity of the smelters to cut costs and re-deploy its redundant work-force in losing mines to viable mines.
The company should close down unviable mines in phases, and boost activity in more economical open-cast mines, he said. Concentrates could be imported if they are cheaper, he added.
India has around 205 known deposits of copper but the quality of the ore is poor. The recovery rate is about 1.2 to 1.3 percent compared with 2.3 percent worldwide.
The disinvestment panel suggested two alternative routes for the partial privatisation of HCL.

Under the first, HCL may select a strategic partner through a competitive bidding process to offer 51 percent of the company's equity, and sell 23 percent to employees, small investors and domestic institutions, the panel said.

The other option would be to initially sell off 51 percent to a strategic partner and then implement a restructuring operation, after which the government could sell 23 percent to employees, small investors and institutions, it said.
The panel said the government must retain a 26 percent stake in HCL in view of the strategic importance of copper mining.
HCL has nine underground mines and one open-cast mine with a total smelting capacity of 47,500 tonnes per annum.
The company reported losses of 1.3 billion rupees in fiscal 1996/97 (April-March) due to a lowering of customs duties on copper and highly volatile prices on the LME.
But it reported a gross profit of 130 million rupees in April-June 1997, mainly on account of higher LME prices.

"The future of the company is dependent vitally on the immediate implementation of the expansion project and any delay will lead to the company turning sick over the next two years, especially in view of the current depressed copper prices in the LME," the Disinvestment Commission said.
